title: Deterministic divisibility testing by a constant-degree polynomial
formal: For every fixed integer \(\delta \ge 2\), is there a deterministic algorithm using \(\operatorname{poly}(n,s,d)\) arithmetic operations over Q that, given an explicitly s-sparse polynomial \(f\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) of total degree at most d and a nonzero polynomial \(g\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) of total degree at most \(\delta\), decides whether g divides f?
context:
This problem verifies one supplied potential divisor. It does not ask to discover all irreducible factors or to decide whether f itself is irreducible. The nonlinear candidate can already be quadratic.

For example, \(x^{D}- 1\) is sparse and divisible by \(x- 1\), but its quotient has D terms. Sparsity of f therefore gives no promise that a quotient has few monomials relative to the sparse input length.

Deterministic polynomial-time testing is available for linear divisors; for arbitrary fixed-degree nonlinear divisors, the cited general sparse-dividend result is quasipolynomial. The target removes that quasipolynomial overhead.

The 2026 result gives polynomial time when every variable’s degree in the dividend is a fixed constant. Here only the divisor g has fixed total degree: the dividend can have arbitrarily large individual degrees up to d.
why: Tests whether even a supplied low-degree factor of a sparse multivariate polynomial can be verified efficiently without randomness, a basic obstruction in deterministic factorization.
status_note: Source field, cost model and missing predicate checked, together with the 2024 full-version record, the 2026 bounded-individual-degree result and arXiv:2606.12130 on finite-field sparse divisibility. The latter uses a different field and unrestricted divisor degrees. No resolution of this fixed-degree-divisor rational-arithmetic target was located through 12 September 2026.

progress.text: Forbes gives deterministic quasipolynomial-time divisibility testing for constant-degree divisors of sparse polynomials.
Dutta, Sinhababu and Thierauf retain polynomial-time testing as open even for quadratic divisors.
Chuyoon and Shpilka give new factorization guarantees under bounded individual degree of the dividend, while distinguishing the unrestricted case.

references.title: Derandomizing Multivariate Polynomial Factoring for Low Degree Factors
references.authors: Dutta, Pranjal; Sinhababu, Amit; Thierauf, Thomas
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 14; PDF page 14

definitions: A sparse representation of f lists its nonzero rational coefficients and corresponding nonnegative integer exponent vectors; s is the number of listed monomials and d bounds the sum of exponents in each monomial. The candidate divisor g is supplied by its coefficients and exponent vectors; because \(\delta\) is fixed, it has at most \(binomial(n+\delta ,\delta )\) monomials, so dense and sparse explicit encodings are polynomially related. Divisibility means that a polynomial \(h\in Q[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}]\) exists with \(f=gh\). The quotient need not be sparse and need not be output. The polynomial running-time exponent may depend on the fixed \(\delta\), but not on the input n,s,d. The source counts exact arithmetic operations over Q at unit cost. In particular, the requested bound is polynomial in the numerical degree d, not merely in log d, and is not a bound on rational-coefficient bit complexity. There is no promise that g is irreducible. The cases \(f=0\) or nonzero constant g have immediate affirmative answers; the first unsettled divisor degree is two.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic divisibility decision algorithm with the stated polynomial arithmetic cost for every fixed \(\delta\), or establish an obstruction to that precise guarantee. Randomized testing, quasipolynomial time, or a bound requiring the dividend f to have constant individual degree does not answer the question.
